title: Global Consensus Recommendations on Prevention and Management of Nutritional Rickets
authors: Munns CF, Shaw N, Kiely M, Specker BL, Thacher TD, Ozono K, et al.
journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
funder: Financially supported by the participating societies listed in the paper and by an educational grant (non-participatory) from Danone Nutricia.
authorConflicts: M.Z.M. has received honoraria and lecture fees from Nutricia and Alexion; W.H. from Internis and Alexion; T.D.T. is a consultant for Biomedical Systems; no other author has anything to disclose.
result: Vitamin D status by serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D: sufficiency above 50 nmol/L, insufficiency 30 to 50 nmol/L, deficiency below 30 nmol/L; toxicity defined as hypercalcaemia with 25-hydroxyvitamin D above 250 nmol/L, hypercalciuria and suppressed PTH. Nutritional rickets is caused by vitamin D deficiency and/or low calcium intake; in children over 12 months, dietary calcium below 300 mg/day increases the risk of rickets independent of serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D. 400 IU/day (10 µg) is adequate to prevent rickets and is recommended for all infants from birth to 12 months. Recommendations graded with the GRADE system.
